AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To describe the presence, frequency, severity, and distress of symptoms in outpatients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma toward the end of life, and the variability in psychological and physical symptom distress between and within patients over time.  .

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Outpatient clinics at two healthcare institutions.  .

AbstractText.Label: SAMPLE
AbstractText.content: 18 patients (15 men and 3 women) with hepatocellular carcinoma and a mean age of 63.3 years (range = 54-81 years). .

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Data were collected monthly for six months. Patients completed the Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale, which reports a total score, and three subscales that provide global distress, psychological distress, and physical distress scores. .

AbstractText.Label: FINDINGS
AbstractText.content: Patients reported lack of energy and pain as the most frequent and distressing symptoms. Problems with sexual interest or activity was the fourth most present symptom after drowsiness. Global Distress Index mean scores had notable variability between and within patients over time. During data collection, six patients died. None were referred to palliative care. .

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Gaining knowledge about symptom distress and prevalent symptoms experienced by patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma is critical for designing symptom management strategies that are comprehensive and tailored to patients to optimize their quality of life as they approach death. .

AbstractText.Label: IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING
AbstractText.content: Nurses play a vital role in advocating for, initiating, and providing comprehensive holistic care based on individual patient needs by facilitating discussions about apparent and less apparent distressing symptoms, including those related to sexuality.

Article.ArticleTitle: Symptom Distress in Patients With Hepatocellular Carcinoma Toward the End of Life.
